transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look, especially since I started helping with the safety trainings and I’m pointing things out. And in the newsletter photos, I keep thinking my face looks crooked. Other people say they don’t see it, but I do.
When others tell you they don't notice any unevenness or crookedness, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or do you feel completely certain that what you're seeing is real?

I know they’re telling me they don’t see it, but when I look at the photos, my face still looks crooked to me. And when I’m pointing during the trainings, I notice every wrinkle and uneven part of my hands. It’s hard for me to believe they really don’t see it.
On a scale from 'I know for certain this is true' to 'I think this is true but I could be wrong,' how would you describe your level of certainty about your face or hands looking abnormal?

I think it’s true, but I suppose I could be wrong. Other people keep saying they don’t notice it. Still, when I’m looking at the newsletter pictures or seeing my hands while I’m pointing things out, it looks very clear to me.

latest_inference.note: Patient acknowledges possible inaccuracy of perception ('I could be wrong') despite subjective clarity, indicating fair/partial insight rather than fixed delusional certainty, which argues against a primary psychotic disorder (F22) and supports body dysmorphic disorder with fair insight (F45.22).

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports persistent preoccupation with perceived flaws in facial symmetry and hand skin texture, which are not observable or only slightly noticeable to others. She engages in repetitive checking behaviors (scrutinizing photos, examining hands while pointing) and has some insight, acknowledging she 'could be wrong' though the perceived defects still feel very real to her. This pattern of specific body-focused preoccupation with checking behaviors and fair insight is consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22) rather than a delusional disorder (fixed, unshakeable belief) or generalized hypochondriasis about illness (F45.21).
